fetched_contents.text: A review of analytical methods for assessing preservation in waterlogged archaeological wood and their application in practice Introduction and background Assessing the current state of preservation of waterlogged archaeological wood provides vital information on decay trajectories, archaeological significance (the state of preservation is likely to influence the level of detail that can be retrieved from an object), and the potential consequences of changing conditions [1, 2]. Appropriate analysis establishes a robust baseline against which any further deterioration can be tracked, for example: when a site is being monitored [3, 4], when comparing material from different sites or phases of investigation [5, 6], or when gathering experimental data on decay mechanisms [7,8,9]. Analysis is also important post-excavation; detecting decay over periods of storage or display can help identify when conditions are not conducive to the continued survival of an object [10, 11]. Analysis during or after conservation can be a critical part of establishing when a conservation treatment has worked, or indeed is having a negative effect [12, 13]. Understanding the structure of wood, the potential decay mechanisms acting upon it, and appropriate techniques that can be used to assess and track these mechanisms is therefore important for archaeologists, conservators, and heritage management professionals. The structure and decay of waterlogged archaeological wood Fresh wood is made up of a system of cells composed of three major biopolymers, closely linked and arranged in fibrils (Fig. 1). The first of these, lignin, composes roughly 25–35% by mass, whilst cellulose and hemi-celluloses (two types of polysaccharide) together make up roughly 65–75%. A variety of ‘extractives’ (non-structural components such as pectins, tannins, resins, and oils) contribute up to 10% by mass. An in-depth description of the anatomical structure of wood is outside the scope of this review but can be found in e.g. [14,15,16]. Archaeological wood is subjected to a variety of both chemical and biological decay processes during its deposition and burial, resulting in a material with a very different chemical composition and structure to fresh wood [14, 17]. Under the anoxic conditions provided by waterlogged environments, decay processes are significantly slowed and primarily driven by anaerobic biological agents [15, 18, 19]. These agents preferentially attack polysaccharides via enzymatic degradation, with hemi-celluloses being particularly vulnerable [15, 20]. Some studies demonstrate that chemical deterioration of cellulose also occurs in waterlogged environments, particularly under extreme conditions such as low pH [6, 10]. Lignin is generally considered to be much more resistant to biological decay, largely due to its highly stable structure: a large 3 dimensional network of cross-linked polyphenol sub units (Fig. 1; [20]. The preferential decay of celluloses means that waterlogged archaeological wood is often characterised by a high lignin content, with celluloses completely depleted in some cases [21, 22]. In waterlogged environments, the cellulose-depleted cell walls become instead filled with water, allowing the structure of the wood to be maintained [20]. However, this lignin-rich skeleton is a very fragile material that is highly susceptible to mechanical damage and can collapse or warp very easily when dried [12, 23]. Although comparatively stable, decay of lignin does also occur. In particular, certain anaerobic fungi digest lignin via enzymatic oxidation [15, 21]. This results in modification of the sub-units, for example an increased concentration of the more resistant guaiacyl-type lignin compared to syringyl-type is often observed in decayed wood [16, 17]. Exchange with the burial environment can influence the chemical composition of waterlogged archaeological wood. Many ‘extractives’ are water soluble, and therefore present in drastically lower concentrations or completely absent [14, 17]. The highly porous nature of wood means that minerals from the burial environment (such as iron sulfides, phosphates and calcium) may become incorporated into the cell walls over time, resulting in a higher inorganic, or ‘ash’ content [17, 24]. A particularly problematic process is the build-up of sulfur salts in wood from marine environments, as these can oxidise when exposed to air and form sulfuric acid, leading to subsequent hydrolysis of cellulose [25, 26]. The presence of iron (e.g. from nails) alongside sulfur in particular can lead to the formation of a wide range of salts within the cellular structure, which leads to extensive mechanical damage if they occupy more volume than the precursor molecules [26, 27]. The identification of inorganic components can be critical for predicting the success of conservation treatments and the possible effects of long-term storage. Challenges in the analysis of waterlogged archaeological wood Analysis of waterlogged archaeological wood aims to evaluate these chemical and physical changes in order to determine its current state of preservation. This knowledge is vital in informing conservation or management of these objects: an adequate assessment supplies a baseline against which future change can be measured, and provides an indication of whether further changes might be expected as a result of the proposed strategy [1, 12]. However, the complexity of waterlogged archaeological wood, particularly its highly heterogeneous nature, presents significant analytical challenges. As deterioration tends to occur first at the surface and progress inwards there is often a gradient of decay, with the inner heartwood much better preserved than the outer sapwood [12, 15]. Different species of erosion microorganisms will also result in different patterns of decay [15]. fetched_contents.text: Physicochemical structure and micromechanical properties of archaeological wood under alternating dry and wet conditions: Wood Material Science & Engineering: Vol 19, No 3 ABSTRACT The relationship between physicochemical structure and micromechanical properties of archaeological wood is not understand. For this purpose, the study took the archaeological wood from the Shahe Ancient Bridge site as an example. The physical properties, microstructure, chemical composition, and micromechanics of archaeological wood were evaluated using non-destructive and micro-destructive techniques. The results indicated that the deterioration of Phoebe sp. wood was more severe than that of Abies sp. wood. However, the basic density of Phoebe sp. wood was higher than that of the control sample due to the collapse of cell walls. The cell walls exhibited a variety of destructional forms, such as cavities and collapses, caused by decay fungi and erosion bacteria. The cell cavities and cell walls deposited inorganic substances. Furthermore, hemicellulose and amorphous cellulose were preferentially degraded before crystalline cellulose was degraded, and S-type lignin was more prone to degradation compared to G-type lignin. Due to the changes of cell wall structure, the hardness of the cell walls increased while the elastic modulus of the cell wall decreased significantly. This study may provide a reference for the study of the relationship between cell wall structure and micromechanics of archaeological wood. fetched_contents.text: Evaluation of the state of preservation of waterlogged archaeological wood based on its physical properties: basic density vs. wood substance density Introduction The state of preservation of waterlogged archaeological wood is evaluated mainly for the selection of an appropriate method for its conservation. Such a test is performed also in the case of monitoring the ongoing rate of degradation of wood tissue. The degree of wood decomposition can be determined on the basis of its physical and chemical properties as well as by microscopic observations (Babiński, 2005, Capretti et al., 2008, Gregory and Jensen, 2006, Hoffmann et al., 1986, Hoffmann and Parameswaran, 1982, Macchioni et al., 2012, Passialis, 1997, Pizzo et al., 2013, Schniewind, 1990). In many conservation laboratories, evaluation of the state of preservation of archaeological wood tissue is most often based on the physical properties of the wood, related to its mass and volume. This is because it is a simple research method and considerable repeatability of the results can be obtained. The fact that the choice of a method of conservation of waterlogged archaeological wood is mainly based on its physical properties should not be underestimated. Such a procedure has been widely described in many publications, which makes it a valuable source of information for conservators of monuments. On the other hand, no detailed procedures have yet been worked out to enable choosing an appropriate method for dimensional stabilization and strengthening of wood on the basis of the results of its chemical and/or microscopic analyses. Usually, in order to evaluate the degree of degradation of waterlogged wood its maximum moisture content and basic density are considered. To a much lesser extent, decay of the objects to be conserved is evaluated on the basis of wood density in waterlogged condition or porosity (Donato and Lazzara, 2012, Hoffmann and Blanchette, 1997, Mikolaychuk, 1997). However, the application of wood substance density for that purpose has not often been observed. It is widely acknowledged that the mass and volume of wood substance forming the cell walls decreases as the wood decay develops. This process results in a decrease in basic density and wood density in wet condition, as well as an increase in porosity and maximum moisture content. There are strict dependences between all those properties, described in many handbooks on wood science. Practical guidelines for determining the physical properties of waterlogged archaeological wood and the dependences between them were presented in detail by Jensen and Gregory (2006). However, wood is a material the properties of which vary not only with the degree of decomposition of its cell walls. Thermogravimetry is limited by the strong dependence of its outcome on moisture content and rehydration, because waterlogged archaeological wood often contains a large and variable proportion of water, and drying or rehydration can change the mass loss pattern. The cited review notes that waterlogged wood is highly porous and can incorporate minerals and salts from the burial environment, and that water is a major component of the material [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that wood is a heterogeneous material with a gradient of decay, and that different regions of the same sample may have very different states of preservation [N1-F1]. In practice, this means that the moisture content of the sample is not a passive parameter but a central variable that can distort the thermogravimetric curve. For example, the cited case study on preservation evaluation explicitly treats physical properties such as basic density and maximum moisture content as important indicators of decomposition, and notes that moisture content and porosity are strongly interdependent [N5-F3]. A separate source on thermogravimetric analysis of archaeological wood also states that thermal analysis methods are used to study degradation of wood structural components and cellulose, suggesting that the presence of moisture or other volatile components can affect how much mass is lost during heating [N3-R5].

Decomposition products and char formation further complicate interpretation because thermogravimetry measures total mass loss, not the identity of the decomposed components. The review on waterlogged archaeological wood explains that lignin is generally resistant to biological decay, cellulose and hemicellulose are preferentially degraded, and lignin can be modified by anaerobic fungi into more resistant forms [N1-F1]. The same review also notes that sulfur salts can oxidize and form sulfuric acid, which then hydrolyzes cellulose, showing that decomposition products can be both chemical and oxidative in origin [N1-F1]. ## Main limitations of using thermogravimetry to assess the preservation state of archaeological wood

Thermogravimetry (TG) is a useful screening tool for studying the thermal degradation behavior of archaeological wood, but it has several important limitations that make it an incomplete or unreliable standalone diagnostic for preservation state. The limitations fall into four broad categories: **technical and measurement limitations**, **interpretive and contextual limitations**, **practical and archaeological constraints**, and **limitations of using TG as a standalone diagnostic**. These are not separate flaws, but interconnected weaknesses that arise from the nature of the material and the method.

---

### 1. Technical and measurement limitations

#### Moisture content and rehydration strongly affect outcomes

The review also notes that sulfur salts can oxidize and form sulfuric acid, which then hydrolyzes cellulose, showing that decomposition products can be both chemical and oxidative in origin [N1-F1]. This means that TG results can be ambiguous because they may reflect post-mortem chemical damage as well as genuine preservation state.

TG is highly sensitive to experimental conditions, so sample size, heating rate, and atmosphere can strongly affect reproducibility. The review on waterlogged wood further notes that analysis aims to evaluate chemical and physical changes, implying that the atmosphere and heating conditions used in TG will affect the measured decomposition trajectory [N1-F1]. The review on analytical methods for waterlogged wood states that the material is highly heterogeneous and that deterioration tends to occur first at the surface and progress inward [N1-F1]. Mechanical or physical testing complements TG results by providing information about strength, density, and dimensional stability. The review on analytical methods for waterlogged wood notes that the state of preservation is evaluated for conservation and for monitoring ongoing degradation [N1-F1]. The review on complementary methods states that mechanical testing provides rapid, in situ evaluation of residual strength, and that physico-mechanical properties can be correlated with chemistry [N6-R2; N6-R5]. TG is useful where mass-loss behavior is informative, but it is insufficient where preservation is heterogeneous, charred, or influenced by non-wood components. TG is useful for identifying the onset and progression of decomposition because it measures total mass loss as a function of temperature [N1-F1; N3-R5]. The review on complementary methods further notes that mechanical testing and microscopy are often used to support conservation decisions, which implies that TG should be used alongside them rather than as a replacement [N6-R2]. In short, TG is a powerful tool for screening or comparative analysis, but it is not a complete diagnostic on its own [N1-F1; N3-R5; N6-R2].

---

## Conclusion

Overall, the main limitations of using thermogravimetry to assess the preservation state of archaeological wood are:

- **Technical limitations**: moisture content and rehydration strongly affect outcomes; decomposition products and char formation complicate interpretation; sample size, heating rate, and atmosphere influence reproducibility [N1-F1; N5-F3; N3-R5; N2-R3; N3-R1].
- **Interpretive limitations**: preserved, degraded, and charred wood are difficult to distinguish; preservation state is not uniquely determined by a single TG curve; interpretation depends on prior knowledge of burial environment and treatment history [N1-F1; N2-R3; N5-F3].
- **Practical and archaeological constraints**: sample preparation is difficult because the material is fragile, heterogeneous, and contaminated; contamination and reagent interference risks are real; TG is not a standalone preservation diagnostic [N1-F1; N5-F3; N3-R1].
- **Complementary methods and comparison**: microscopy and chemical analysis provide additional clues; mechanical or physical testing complements TG results; TG is useful for screening and baseline monitoring, but insufficient for definitive preservation assessment [N6-R2; N1-F1; N4-F2; N5-F3; N3-R5].

Because of these limitations, thermogravimetry should be treated as one part of a broader analytical toolkit rather than as a definitive diagnostic for archaeological wood preservation [N1-F1; N5-F3; N6-R2].

## Main limitations of using thermogravimetry to assess the preservation state of archaeological wood

Thermogravimetry (TG) is a useful screening tool for studying the thermal degradation behavior of archaeological wood, but it has several important limitations that make it an incomplete or unreliable standalone diagnostic for preservation state. The limitations fall into four broad categories: **technical and measurement limitations**, **interpretive and contextual limitations**, **practical and archaeological constraints**, and **limitations of using TG as a standalone diagnostic**. These are not separate flaws, but interconnected weaknesses that arise from the nature of the material and the method.

### 1. Technical and measurement limitations

#### Moisture content and rehydration strongly affect outcomes
Thermogravimetry is highly sensitive to moisture content because waterlogged archaeological wood often contains a large and variable proportion of water. The review on waterlogged archaeological wood explains that the material is highly porous and can incorporate minerals and salts from the burial environment, while also noting that water is a major component of the material [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that wood is a heterogeneous material with a gradient of decay, so the moisture content is not a passive parameter but a central variable that can distort the thermogravimetric curve [N1-F1]. The case study on preservation evaluation explicitly treats basic density and maximum moisture content as important indicators of decomposition, and notes that moisture content and porosity are strongly interdependent [N5-F3]. This means that a sample’s TG outcome can change dramatically if it is rehydrated, dried, or otherwise altered after sampling.

#### Decomposition products and char formation complicate interpretation
TG measures total mass loss, not the identity of the decomposed components, so it cannot distinguish between original wood components and later-formed decomposition products. The same review explains that lignin is generally resistant to biological decay, cellulose and hemicellulose are preferentially degraded, and lignin can be modified by anaerobic fungi into more resistant forms [N1-F1]. These layers can make the TG curve appear to reflect a mixture of degradation states rather than a single preservation condition. The review also notes that sulfur salts can oxidize and form sulfuric acid, which then hydrolyzes cellulose, showing that decomposition products can be both chemical and oxidative in origin [N1-F1]. This means that TG results can be ambiguous because they may reflect post-mortem chemical damage as well as genuine preservation state.

Overall, the main limitations of using thermogravimetry to assess the preservation state of archaeological wood are:

- **Technical limitations**: moisture content and rehydration strongly affect outcomes; decomposition products and char formation complicate interpretation; sample size, heating rate, and atmosphere influence reproducibility [N1-F1; N5-F3; N3-R5; N2-R3; N3-R1].

## Main limitations of using thermogravimetry to assess the preservation state of archaeological wood

The limitations fall into four broad categories: **technical and measurement limitations**, **interpretive and contextual limitations**, **practical and archaeological constraints**, and **limitations of using TG as a standalone diagnostic**. These are not separate flaws, but interconnected weaknesses that arise from the nature of the material and the method.

---

### 1. Technical and measurement limitations

#### Moisture content and rehydration strongly affect outcomes
Thermogravimetry is highly sensitive to moisture content because waterlogged archaeological wood often contains a large and variable proportion of water. The review on waterlogged archaeological wood explains that the material is highly porous and can incorporate minerals and salts from the burial environment, while also noting that water is a major component of the material [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that wood is a heterogeneous material with a gradient of decay, so the moisture content is not a passive parameter but a central variable that can distort the thermogravimetric curve [N1-F1]. The case study on preservation evaluation explicitly treats basic density and maximum moisture content as important indicators of decomposition, and notes that moisture content and porosity are strongly interdependent [N5-F3]. This means that a sample’s TG outcome can change dramatically if it is rehydrated, dried, or otherwise altered after sampling.

#### Decomposition products and char formation complicate interpretation
TG measures total mass loss, not the identity of the decomposed components, so it cannot distinguish between original wood components and later-formed decomposition products. The same review explains that lignin is generally resistant to biological decay, cellulose and hemicellulose are preferentially degraded, and lignin can be modified by anaerobic fungi into more resistant forms [N1-F1]. In charred wood, the formation of char and pyrolysis products creates distinct layers, including a charred layer, charring base, pyrolysis layer, and intact wood [N2-R3]. These layers can make the TG curve appear to reflect a mixture of degradation states rather than a single preservation condition. The review also notes that sulfur salts can oxidize and form sulfuric acid, which then hydrolyzes cellulose, showing that decomposition products can be both chemical and oxidative in origin [N1-F1]. This means that TG results can be ambiguous because they may reflect post-mortem chemical damage as well as genuine preservation state.

#### Sample size, heating rate, and atmosphere influence reproducibility
TG is highly sensitive to experimental conditions, so sample size, heating rate, and atmosphere can strongly affect reproducibility. The review on waterlogged wood notes that the material is highly heterogeneous and that deterioration tends to occur first at the surface and progress inward, creating a gradient of decay [N1-F1]. This heterogeneity means that small samples may not represent the whole object, and reproducibility depends on sampling strategy [N5-F3]. The cited thermogravimetric analysis of ancient and fresh woods was applied to samples from portals of old churches and other archaeological materials, indicating that the method has been used but is still subject to sample-specific variation [N3-R1]. The case study on preservation evaluation also states that the accuracy of physical-property measurements is influenced by small amounts of air remaining in wet wood, excess water on the sample surface, and over-drying [N5-F3]. The review on waterlogged wood further notes that analysis aims to evaluate chemical and physical changes, implying that the atmosphere and heating conditions used in TG will affect the measured decomposition trajectory [N1-F1]. Taken together, these sources show that TG results are not robust unless the sample is prepared carefully and the conditions are controlled [N1-F1; N3-R1; N5-F3].

---

### 2. Interpretive and contextual limitations

#### Difficulty distinguishing preserved, degraded, and charred wood
One of the main interpretive challenges is that thermogravimetric curves do not provide a unique signature for each preservation state. The review on waterlogged wood explains that decay processes vary by species and burial environment, and that different erosion microorganisms can produce different decay patterns [N1-F1]. It also notes that the inner heartwood is often better preserved than the outer sapwood, while localized differences in burial environment can cause regions of more decayed wood [N1-F1]. This heterogeneity means that a single TG curve may reflect a composite of different preservation conditions rather than a single state. The cited review on charred wood also shows that surface carbonization produces distinct layers: charred layer, charring base, pyrolysis layer, and intact wood [N2-R3]. If these layers are present, the TG curve will show multiple mass-loss steps, making it hard to assign the result unambiguously to preservation state rather than to the presence of char or pyrolytic products [N2-R3]. In addition, the review on waterlogged wood notes that sulfur salts can oxidize and form sulfuric acid, which hydrolyzes cellulose, indicating that degradation can be both chemical and oxidative [N1-F1]. These multiple mechanisms imply that TG alone cannot reliably separate preservation from post-mortem chemical damage.

#### Preservation state is not uniquely determined by a single TG curve
A single TG curve is not enough to determine preservation state because the material’s chemistry is highly variable. The review on analytical methods for waterlogged wood states that analysis is important for conservation or management because it provides a baseline against which future change can be measured, and that the state of preservation is likely to influence the level of detail that can be retrieved from an object [N1-F1]. It also notes that the complexity of waterlogged wood, particularly its highly heterogeneous nature, presents significant analytical challenges [N1-F1]. The case study on preservation evaluation further states that basic density and maximum moisture content are often used to assess decomposition, but that these properties vary with sampling place, tree growth conditions, and natural defects, and that comparing archaeological fragments to fresh-material averages can be unreliable [N5-F3]. This suggests that a single TG curve must be interpreted alongside other physical and chemical properties, because the same mass-loss pattern could arise from different combinations of cell-wall loss, water content, and mineral content [N1-F1; N5-F3]. The review on analytical methods also emphasizes that appropriate analysis establishes a robust baseline for tracking deterioration, which implies that TG is most useful when combined with repeated measurements and contextual information [N1-F1].

#### Dependence on prior knowledge of burial environment and treatment history
TG is not a self-contained diagnostic because it depends on prior knowledge of the burial environment and treatment history. The review on waterlogged wood explains that exchange with the burial environment can influence chemical composition, because many extractives are water soluble and may be absent or present in lower concentrations [N1-F1]. It also notes that minerals from the burial environment may become incorporated into the cell walls, increasing the inorganic or ash content [N1-F1]. The case study on preservation evaluation states that the choice of conservation method is mainly based on physical properties, and that such a procedure has been widely described in many publications, but that no detailed procedures exist for choosing conservation based on chemical or microscopic analyses [N5-F3]. This means that without knowing the burial environment, the presence of salts, sulfur compounds, or other inorganic components can distort the TG interpretation [N1-F1]. Similarly, the review on analytical methods notes that the structure of wood and the potential decay mechanisms acting upon it are important for choosing appropriate techniques, so the analyst must know the likely history of the object before assigning a preservation state to a TG curve [N1-F1]. In short, TG is not a standalone diagnostic because it requires contextual knowledge of the object’s burial history and conservation treatment to avoid misinterpretation [N1-F1; N5-F3].

### 3. Practical and archaeological constraints

#### Sample preparation challenges in archaeological contexts
Sample preparation is a major constraint in archaeological contexts because the material is often fragile, heterogeneous, and contaminated. The review on waterlogged archaeological wood explains that waterlogged wood is highly porous and can incorporate minerals such as iron sulfides, phosphates, and calcium, increasing the inorganic or ash content [N1-F1]. It also notes that sulfur salts can oxidize and form sulfuric acid, which hydrolyzes cellulose, and that iron and sulfur can form a wide range of salts that cause mechanical damage if they occupy more volume than the precursor molecules [N1-F1]. The case study on preservation evaluation states that the physical properties of archaeological wood are often measured using small, irregular samples, and that the accuracy of measurements is influenced by air remaining in wet wood, excess surface water, and over-drying [N5-F3]. The review on analytical methods also notes that the material is heterogeneous and that deterioration tends to occur first at the surface and progress inward, so a representative sample is hard to obtain from a single fragment [N1-F1].

Contamination and reagent interference are important because thermogravimetry involves heating in a controlled atmosphere and can be sensitive to foreign substances. The review on waterlogged wood states that minerals from the burial environment may become incorporated into the cell walls, and that extractives may be absent or present in lower concentrations [N1-F1]. It also notes that sulfur salts can oxidize and form sulfuric acid, which hydrolyzes cellulose, indicating that decomposition products can be chemically reactive and interfere with interpretation [N1-F1]. Still, the general principle is clear: if the sample has been exposed to salts, oxidants, or other burial-phase materials, those substances can alter the mass-loss profile during heating [N1-F1]. The review on analytical methods further notes that the structure of wood and the potential decay mechanisms are important for choosing appropriate techniques, so any reagent or atmosphere used in TG must not introduce new reactions that mask the true decomposition behavior [N1-F1].
